candidates.attacker_control: A remote HTTP client supplies the value: the MVC controller copies every request header into the FunctionWrapper (FunctionController.wrapper lines 125-131) and FunctionWebRequestProcessingHelper.processRequest line 92 builds the input message with `MessageBuilder.withPayload(argument).copyHeaders(headers.toSingleValueMap())`; the WebFlux controller does the same (flux/FunctionController lines 99-105). In Lambda deployments, AWSLambdaUtils.generateMessage copies the API-Gateway `headers` map into message headers (lines 132-136). No name/value filtering is applied to the request path: HeaderUtils only strips headers for responses (`sanitize`, IGNORED/REQUEST_ONLY lists), not for the inbound message, and MessageUtils.copyHeaders performs no filtering.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked (a) whether the header is filtered anywhere: HeaderUtils.IGNORED/REQUEST_ONLY (lines 34-46) and sanitize() (lines 67-77) only affect response headers; the inbound message copies all headers unfiltered; (b) whether the trusted property path masks the header: the header branch at lines 125-130 is evaluated before functionProperties.getRoutingExpression() (lines 131-133), so it does not; (c) whether evaluation is sandboxed: the field at line 60 is a full StandardEvaluationContext, not SimpleEvaluationContext, and the 4-arg constructor in ContextFunctionCatalogAutoConfiguration sets a BeanFactoryResolver; (d) whether the routing function is a real registered target: @Bean(RoutingFunction.FUNCTION_NAME) functionRouter is registered unconditionally and FunctionCatalog.lookup resolves it by name; (e) whether other SpEL usages are reachable from attacker input: HeaderEnricher expressions come from FunctionRegistration configuration (not request data), FunctionArchiveDeployer uses fixed expressions; (f) searched for other sinks (ProcessBuilder, ObjectInputStream, Runtime.exec, enableDefaultTyping, ScriptEngine) - none present. SpEL evaluation itself was not executed and the snapshot contains no test sources to cross-check intended behavior.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary SpEL evaluation of an attacker-supplied header: method/constructor invocation and bean access in the application JVM, i.e. code execution with the function's privileges (command execution, file access, SSRF, credential/secret access in the deployed context). Even without command execution, it enables forced invocation of arbitrary registered functions/beans and information disclosure through expression evaluation.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses spring-cloud-function-web (or another adapter/messaging binder that lets a publisher set message headers) and the routing gateway is actually engaged for the request, e.g. the request path resolves to the registered `functionRouter` bean (ContextFunctionCatalogAutoConfiguration.functionRouter) or the app is configured with spring.cloud.function.definition=functionRouter; an input Message must reach RoutingFunction (POST with a non-null body, or GET with a path argument). The attacker must be able to set a header whose name is the literal `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression`. No application-specific configuration or privileges are needed beyond reaching the endpoint.
candidates.root_cause: RoutingFunction.route() treats the message header `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` as a SpEL expression and passes it to functionFromExpression(), which calls `spelParser.parseExpression(routingExpression)` and `expression.getValue(this.evalContext, input, String.class)` using a fully featured `StandardEvaluationContext` (line 60) configured with an `MapAccessor` and a `BeanResolver` (lines 79-80). Nothing validates, allowlists or escapes the header value; `StringUtils.hasText` only checks non-emptiness. The header branch (lines 125-130) also precedes the trusted-property branches, so an operator-set `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression`/`definition` property cannot mask an injected header.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled message header `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` is evaluated as SpEL in RoutingFunction (untrusted expression injection / potential RCE)
candidates.trace: HTTP request header -> mvc FunctionController.wrapper (lines 125-128) / flux FunctionController.wrapper (lines 102-105) -> FunctionWrapper.headers -> FunctionWebRequestProcessingHelper.processRequest line 92 MessageBuilder.copyHeaders(headers.toSingleValueMap()) -> FunctionInvocationWrapper.apply/doApply (SimpleFunctionRegistry lines 546/690-698, routing function keeps the Message because isExtractPayload() is false for routing functions) -> RoutingFunction.apply (line 84) -> route() line 125 reads header -> functionFromExpression(routingExpression, message) (line 208) -> SpelExpressionParser.parseExpression (line 209) -> Expression.getValue(StandardEvaluationContext) (line 210) where the context is a plain StandardEvaluationContext with a bean resolver, so type references and method calls in the header value are resolved at runtime.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: I did not start the application, send a request, or evaluate any payload. The exact preconditions of a given deployment (whether the router is exposed at a reachable path/handler and whether an upstream proxy/gateway strips dotted header names) are deployment-specific and were not verified. I also did not verify that every HTTP server/framework version involved accepts the dotted header name over the wire, and I did not inspect compiled artifacts (none present).
candidates.weakness_type: Expression-language injection: untrusted input used as SpEL expression (unsafe expression evaluation, leading to arbitrary code execution)

summary: Spring Cloud Function 3.1.7-SNAPSHOT snapshot. The strongest issue found is an untrusted-expression (SpEL) injection path in the routing gateway: `RoutingFunction` reads the message header `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` and evaluates it as a SpEL expression against an unrestricted `StandardEvaluationContext` (with a BeanFactoryResolver attached). In the `spring-cloud-function-web` modules (both the MVC and the WebFlux controllers) every inbound HTTP request header is copied verbatim into the input Message headers, so a remote client controls the expression string. The same pattern exists in the AWS adapter, which copies API-Gateway request headers into Message headers. Because the context is a full `StandardEvaluationContext` (not `SimpleEvaluationContext`), the expression can reference types and call methods, i.e. arbitrary code execution in the function JVM under the application's privileges. Confidence in the source evidence is high; runtime exploitability/preconditions (routing function actually being served) were not executed.
